label: Research & statistics
summary: The cross-cutting method shelf: every statistical method the engine can run, linked from every subject.
start_steps: Compare groups: Welch two-sample t-test, Mann-Whitney U, One-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis.
Relate variables: Pearson or Spearman correlation, Linear regression or Logistic regression.
Check the design: Power and sample size, Multiple-comparison correction and Missing-data bounds.
does_not: It does not design the study, choose the hypothesis or clean the data for you.
It does not prove causality from observational data.
It does not replace a statistician for a complex or clustered design.
guidance: This is the cross-cutting method shelf. Start with the design and the data shape, then choose the test. Every output states its assumptions, its checks and what it cannot establish; a significant result is not a causal claim.

tools.label: Descriptive statistics
tools.what: Record the count, centre, spread and declared missing-value handling for one variable.
tools.need: the numbers you hold and the group they describe
tools.formula: Mean = sum of values / count; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Spearman rank correlation
tools.what: Record the rank association between two variables without assuming a linear shape.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Linear regression (HC3)
tools.what: The same regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
tools.formula: The same OLS coefficients with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
steps: Fit the same model as OLS.
Read the robust standard errors and their tests.
Compare with the ordinary OLS errors to see whether heteroskedasticity mattered.
Keep the model specification fixed when comparing.
common_mistakes: Thinking robust errors fix a misspecified model.
Comparing robust errors with a different sample or specification.
Using HC3 as a substitute for checking outliers.
Reporting robust errors without saying which correction was used.

tools.label: Welch two-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare two group means without assuming equal variances.
tools.formula: t = (mean A - mean B) / standard error of the difference, without assuming equal variances.
steps: Check the two groups are independent.
Read the difference, the interval and the p-value together.
Report the effect size, not only significance.
common_mistakes: Treating a small p-value as a large effect.
Using a paired test for independent groups.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Mann-Whitney U test
tools.what: Compare two groups by rank when the distributional assumption is not met.

tools.label: One-way ANOVA
tools.what: Compare three or more group means and record the effect size and checks.
tools.formula: F = between-group variance / within-group variance.
steps: Check the groups are independent.
Read the F test and the effect size.
Use a post-hoc test before naming which groups differ.
common_mistakes: Running several t-tests instead of one ANOVA.
Naming the winning group from the omnibus test alone.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
tools.what: Compare three or more groups by rank, the non-parametric alternative to ANOVA.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Two-way ANOVA
tools.what: Record the two main effects and their interaction with the frozen checks.

tools.label: Post-hoc pairwise tests
tools.what: Compare group pairs after a significant omnibus test, with the correction declared.

tools.label: Multiple-comparison correction
tools.what: Correct a declared family of tests and show the adjusted decisions.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Missing-data bounds
tools.what: Bound how far the missing values could move the mean, without imputing them.
tools.formula: The mean is bounded by valuing every missing observation at the minimum and at the maximum observed value; the bound width shows how much the missing data could move it.
steps: Enter the observations you have, leaving missing values blank or marking their codes.
Declare the missing-data mechanism you believe applies; it is recorded, not verified.
Read the complete-case mean and the worst-case bounds.
Report the bound beside the estimate, not instead of it.
common_mistakes: Treating the bound as a confidence interval.
Assuming the missing values are random without evidence.
Dropping incomplete rows and reporting the mean as if nothing were missing.
Using a missing code as a real observation.

tools.label: Paired t-test
tools.what: Compare paired before/after measurements on the same units.

tools.label: One-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare a sample mean with a declared target.

tools.label: Logistic regression
tools.what: Fit a declared binary-outcome model and record coefficients and fit checks.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.

tools.label: Weighted summary
tools.what: Summarise scores with the design weights you supply, stating the weighting rule.
tools.need: the values you want to weigh and the weights you are declaring
tools.formula: Weighted mean = sum(weight x value) / sum(weight); design effect = (n - 1) / (n_effective - 1).
steps: Enter one value per line and one weight per line, in the same order.
Declare the kind of weight: frequency, reliability or sampling.
Read the weighted mean and the weighted standard deviation.
Read the effective sample size: how many unweighted observations your weights are worth.
common_mistakes: Entering the values and the weights in a different order.
Leaving the weight kind undeclared, so the two standard deviations cannot be told apart.
Using reliability weights and then treating the result as a population average.
Expecting a confidence interval: this method summarises and does not test.

tools.label: Trend forecast
tools.what: Fit a trend to your own series and record the forecast periods and the range the result could fall in.
tools.need: a series in period order and the horizon
tools.formula: Fit y = a + bt to the series; the forecast extends the line and carries a prediction interval.
steps: Enter the series in order, one value per period.
Declare the horizon you want to forecast.
Read the trend, the forecast values and the interval.
Check the holdout error before trusting the extrapolation.
common_mistakes: Extrapolating far beyond the data without widening the interval.
Ignoring seasonality that a straight line cannot capture.
Reading a high R-squared as proof that the forecast is right.
Forecasting a series that changed regime.
